# McCune-Albright syndrome

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Pediatrics > Important genetic syndromes > McCune-Albright syndrome*

[Original Article Link](/library/VC0GIR)

---

## Summary

McCune-Albright syndrome is a rare genetic disorder that manifests with skeletal, dermatologic, and endocrine abnormalities. It is caused by a <u>G-protein</u> <u>activating mutation</u> that leads to excess production of <u>cAMP</u>. Clinical features include bone <u>pain</u> and/or <u>fractures</u> due to <u>fibrous dysplasia</u>, <u>café-au-lait macules</u>, and <u>peripheral precocious puberty</u>. Other endocrinopathies, such as <u>hyperthyroidism</u>, <u>growth hormone</u> excess, and <u>hypercortisolism</u>, can also occur. Diagnosis is primarily clinical. <u>X-rays</u> showing <u>fibrous dysplasia</u>, abnormal <u>hormone</u> levels on laboratory testing, and <u>genetic testing</u> of affected tissue can help confirm the diagnosis. Management is multidisciplinary and tailored to the specific manifestations of the disease.

---

## Etiology

* <u>Mosaic</u> mutation in the GNAS1 <u>gene</u> on <u>chromosome</u> 20 (<u>autosomal recessive inheritance</u>)

* Some cells have a normal version of the GNAS1 <u>gene</u>, while other cells have the mutated version.

* Embryos only survive if <u>mosaicism</u> occurs.

* If the mutation occurs before <u>fertilization</u>, it affects all cells → incompatible with life.

---

## Pathophysiology

<u>Activating mutation</u> in <u>GNAS gene</u> → impaired <u>G<sub>s</sub>-protein</u> signaling → constitutively activated <u>adenylate cyclase</u> → excess production of <u>cAMP</u> [[2]](/library/T2b6SG)

---

## Clinical features

* Unilateral <u>café-au-lait spots</u> with unilateral, ragged edges

* <u>Polyostotic</u> <u>fibrous dysplasia</u>

* Endocrinopathies

* <u>Peripheral precocious puberty</u> (most common)

* <u>Cushing syndrome</u>

* <u>Acromegaly</u>

* <u>Hyperthyroidism</u>





> [!NOTE]
> The 3 P's of McCune-Albright syndrome are Polyostotic <u>fibrous dysplasia</u>, Pigmentation (<u>café-au-lait spots</u>), and Precocious <u>puberty</u>.

## Diagnosis

* Clinical features: See above.

* Laboratory tests

* Increased <u>hormone</u> levels (e.g., <u>estradiol</u>, <u>testosterone</u>, <u>cortisol</u>, <u>thyroid hormone</u>, <u>growth hormone</u>, <u>prolactin</u>, <u>somatomedin C</u>)

* Increased <u>alkaline phosphatase</u> (see “Diagnostics” in “<u>Fibrous dysplasia</u>”)

* Molecular testing: GNAS1 analysis

* Imaging

* <u>X-rays</u> of <u>long bones</u>: well-defined, lobulated lesions with a thin cortex and a <u>radiolucent</u>, ground-glass appearance

* CT/<u>MRI</u>: identify fibrodysplastic lesions

* <u>Bone scan</u>: determine the extent of bone disease





![Fibrous dysplasia in McCune Albright syndrome](media/a3ewqmfkjdu34vm59x7x5y9p.jpg)

Fibrous dysplasia in McCune Albright syndrome

---

## Treatment

* Symptomatic: treat underlying endocrinopathies

* <u>Estrogen</u> synthesis inhibitors: <u>letrozole</u> [[5]](/library/5cVi1t0)

* <u>Selective estrogen receptor modulators</u> (e.g., <u>tamoxifen</u>)

---

## Prognosis

The condition is lethal when the mutation affects all cells (i.e., occurs before <u>fertilization</u>), but survivable in patients affected by <u>mosaicism</u>.
